sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Adding a basic item is one of the first steps in modding. You're going to need to create an `class_${1}_1792> class.

sections.title: Create an Item instance (before 1.21.2)
sections.summary: :!: If you're in version 1.21.2 or above, please directly read [#Creating Items in 1.21.2+](#Creating Items in 1.21.2+). First, create an instance of `class_${1}_1792`.

sections.title: Register the item (before 1.21.2)
sections.summary: We've create a basic item, but it still does not exist in Minecraft, because it has not been registered. In Minecraft, almost everything has an registry, and items are no exceptions.

sections.title: Best practice of registering items (before 1.21.2)
sections.summary: In the code above, you simply created //one// item. However, it is not convenient if you have //many// items in your mod, as you need to register and create an Identifier instance each time.

sections.title: Creating Items in 1.21.2+
sections.summary: Since 1.21.2, the item registration has been totally rewriten. You have to store a RegistryKey in your Item.Settings, so the models and translation keys will be correctly stored in item components.

sections.title: Adding model, texture and model definition
sections.summary: If you registered your item properly in the first step, you can successfully get your item by typing command /give @s tutorial:custom_item.

sections.title: Creating an Item class
sections.summary: You have created a simple item, and learned how to change some basic properties. But maybe you want it to have more behaviors. Therefore, you will need to create an item class.

sections.title: Item components
sections.summary: Sometimes you may need to add some default components for the item, such as max stack size or fire durability. This can be done by calling component method in Item.Settings.

sections.summary: Try [adding your item to an item group](itemgroup). Your item also does not have a name, so you can also [learn how to add language files](lang).

label: tutorial_commands
firstParagraph: Brigadier is a command parser & dispatcher written by Mojang for use in Minecraft. Brigadier is a tree based command library where you build a tree of arguments and commands.

sections.title: What is Brigadier?
sections.summary: Brigadier is a command parser & dispatcher written by Mojang for use in Minecraft. Brigadier is a tree based command library where you build a tree of arguments and commands.

sections.title: The Command interface
sections.summary: In Minecraft, com.mojang.brigadier.Command is a functional interface, which runs some specific things, and throw a CommandSyntaxException in some cases.

sections.title: Register a basic command
sections.summary: Commands are registered by registering in CommandRegistrationCallback in the Fabric API. For information on registering callbacks, please see the [callbacks](callbacks).

sections.title: Registration environment
sections.summary: If desired, you can also make sure a command is only registered under some specific circumstances, for example, only in the dedicated environment: public class ExampleCommandMod implements ModIniti...

sections.title: Static Imports
sections.summary: In the example above, the use of static imports is used for code simplifying. For a literal this would shorten the statement to `literal("foo")`. This also works for getting the value of an argument.

sections.title: Add Requirements
sections.summary: Let's say you have a command that you only want operators to be able to execute. This is where the requires method comes into play.

sections.title: Arguments
sections.summary: Arguments are used in most of commands. Sometimes they can be optional, which means if you do not provide that argument, the command will also run.
